cur:catacombs-lucina-good-shepherd-wilpe.summary: Within a small painted medallion, a young shepherd in a short belted tunic and leggings stands with a sheep across his shoulders, while a goat stands at his feet and a slender plant rises beside him. In the full ceiling the medallion is framed by a laurel wreath and surrounded by doves and flowering sprigs. The simple pastoral image placed the dead under the care of Christ, the Good Shepherd who seeks the lost and carries them home.
facts: This is Wilpert's plate 35, no. 1, which he described as the ceiling of the 'crypt with the Good Shepherd beneath the Basilica of Silvester' in the Catacomb of Priscilla – 'Good Shepherd, doves, flowering branches' – and dated to the middle of the 4th century.
Pope Silvester I (314–335) built a basilica above the Catacomb of Priscilla; its remains were found in 1890 and partly rebuilt in 1906.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), still the standard illustrated corpus of Roman catacomb painting.

links.label: Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (1903), text volume (Internet Archive)

cur:catacombs-lucina-good-shepherd-wilpe.notes: Corrected location and date, and moved out of the 2nd century: the Commons file is titled 'Calixtus Catacomb, Crypt of Lucina, plate 35', but Wilpert's plate 35 holds two ceilings – no. 1 in the Catacomb of Priscilla (this one: the shepherd in a medallion inside a laurel wreath, with a plant and a goat) and no. 2 in the Crypts of Lucina (a faded shepherd among bowls and birds). Comparison with the plate and Wilpert's list of paintings by catacomb ('Krypta mit der Darstellung des Guten Hirten unter der Silvesterbasilika. Mitte 4. Jht. Taf. 35, 1') shows that the crop is no. 1. The image is a small crop of the 1903 plate; no larger free copy of this ceiling was found on Commons.

cur:manuscripts-trier-apocalypse-son-of-.summary: Christ, tall and haloed, holding a cross-staff, stands among seven tall lampstands with burning flames and stretches out his hand to John, who has fallen at his feet; below, John appears again on the shore of Patmos near a church, with fish in the sea. The page follows the text closely: 'I fell at his feet as dead. And he laid his right hand upon me.'
facts: The Trier Apocalypse contains 74 full-page drawings illustrating about 150 episodes of the Book of Revelation; it is one of the earliest illustrated Apocalypse manuscripts to survive.
Its pictures are thought to copy a late antique model of the 4th–6th century, which explains features such as books shown as scrolls and Christ as the beardless Logos.

walters:W.44.23R.summary: Christ hangs on a green cross against burnished gold, his head bowed and his body slumped in death, while the sun and moon look on from the upper corners. Mary stands at the left with one hand to her cheek and the other raised, and John, holding a book, bows his head at the right. The simple, symmetrical composition and the green 'living wood' of the cross give this small page a quiet, meditative intensity.
facts: The miniature belongs to a ten-image cycle of the Life of Christ added in the 14th century to the front of a 13th-century Psalter (Walters W.44).
The Crucifixion on fol. 23r faces the Flagellation on fol. 22v.
The Psalter's calendar points to Cistercian use, with saints such as Peter of Tarentaise and Malachy.

links.label: The Digital Walters: Psalter for a Cistercian woman (W.44)

walters:W.44.23R.notes: The Walters online record dates this leaf with the whole manuscript to the third quarter of the 13th century, but the Walters' own manuscript description (TEI, The Digital Walters) states that the ten full-page miniatures of the prefatory cycle (fols. 18v–27r) were added in the fourteenth century; the date is corrected accordingly. The worklist year (750) was a parsing error.
